Lundi 11 mars. Le premier ministre d’Haï: Monday, March 11. Haiti’s prime minister, Ariel Henry, resigns. The country has no president and no Parliament, and no election has been held since 2018. Everywhere, Haitians in the diaspora and those living in the country are on edge. No one can predict what comes next, but analysts and activists fear foreign interference during the democratic transition.
Jean Sadrac répond à l’appel vidéo avec: Jean Sadrac answers the video call with cautious enthusiasm, tinged with despair. He arrived in Quebec in 2019, fleeing an already difficult situation in Haiti. The former journalist and communications secretary of his country’s Fusion of Haitian Social Democrats party fears the worst for those he left behind in Port-au-Prince.
« On peut dire que mon corps est au Cana: “You could say my body is in Canada, and that my whole mind, everything that makes me who I am as a human being, lives in Haiti,” he says straight away, sitting at his kitchen table.
Malgré la distance, il reste au fait de: Despite the distance, he stays on top of Haiti’s political life and the situation on the ground. Since Prime Minister Ariel Henry’s resignation, he has been even more alert. Every day, he follows the news, but also social media feeds, where conversations multiply and flare up.
« Être au Québec nous donne une certaine: “Being in Quebec gives us a certain peace, far from the noise of gunfire, but it doesn’t really spare us,” he explains. “Yes, it’s true, we don’t hear the bullets, but when my sister calls me to say she’s under the bed and too afraid to stand up because there are so many projectiles it feels like a country at war, at that moment, I don’t know what to say.”
Affligé, l’ex-journaliste se demande ce: Distraught, the former journalist wonders what will happen. “Anything is possible, given that today, Haiti is not master of itself. If we consider the many foreign interventions in Haiti, what were the results?”
Frantz André, connu pour son travail aup: Frantz André, known for his work with asylum seekers of Haitian origin in Montréal, is in touch with many people in the country. For one of his close friends, it’s panic.
« Un hélicoptère qui est venu chercher d: “A helicopter that came to pick up foreign nationals flew so low that the windows of her house cracked,” says Mr. André, reached by phone. Since then, his friend refuses to leave her home. Her neighbours are the ones bringing her a little food, enough for her and her two children.

Les gens au pays ont peur de parler, rap: People in the country are afraid to speak, say Frantz André and Jean Sadrac. La Converse can corroborate this: it tried to speak with several people on the ground, without success.
Nous avons donc joint Monique*, qui a fu: So we reached Monique*, who fled the country and runs a community organization that helps women and girls who are victims of violence in Port-au-Prince. Fearing reprisals against her family, who remained in the country, and against the centre’s employees, she asked La Converse for anonymity.
« C’est l’instabilité de ce qui est à ve: “It’s the instability of what’s coming that keeps me from being open as an activist for your article,” she says over the phone, as we reached her somewhere in the United States.
Son organisme a dû fermer ses portes tem: Her organization had to close its doors temporarily on March 1<sup>st</sup>. “We have never been able to reopen normally since that date, especially since our offices are downtown. It’s one of the places that are extremely dangerous right now, mainly because public institutions around our space are occupied, or have been occupied or looted, by armed groups,” she recounts.
L’eau est une denrée rare, ainsi que l’a: Water is scarce, as are food and gas.
« Toutes les personnes qui sont à Port-a: “Everyone in Port-au-Prince has a small trunk right next to their bed with all their important papers, money, everything important that can be carried easily at any moment,” says the woman, who also had to leave the country quickly.
Selon l’Organisation des Nations unies,: According to the United Nations, 362,000 people are currently displaced within the country. Some have been displaced more than once, an increase of 15% since the start of the year.
Si les Haïtiens craignent pour leurs pro: While Haitians fear for their loved ones, they also dread what comes next, which could well be marked by an intensification of foreign interference. That is the case for Jemima Pierre.
À la course depuis 5 h du matin en raiso: On the go since 5 a.m. because of interviews she has given to various news networks, the professor catches her breath. She has spent the whole day commenting on Prime Minister Ariel Henry’s resignation. It is 6 p.m. and she has just taught a class at the University of British Columbia. Her conversation with La Converse is online, but her passion transcends the screen.
« Haïti est un laboratoire, car dans que: “Haiti is a laboratory, because in what other state [does this much foreign interference take place] over the past 100 years?” asks the professor in the Global Race department of the Institute of Race, Gender, Sexuality and Social Justice.
Elle estime qu’Haïti est la plus longue: She considers Haiti the longest neo-colonial experiment in the world. Haitian sovereignty was indeed undermined from the very start of the country’s independence. As early as the 19<sup>th</sup> century, France imposed an indemnity of 150 million francs on the country. <l1>The sum was unheard of for the time, but the alternative was war</l1>. Haiti agreed to pay, which locked it into a debt that helped impoverish it.
Puis, en 1914, des Marines américains en: Then, in 1914, American Marines entered Haiti and stole the equivalent of half a million dollars in gold, which they brought back to the United States. The following year, Haiti was invaded by the United States. The occupation would last 19 years.
« Les Américains ont complètement démant: “The Americans completely dismantled the Haitian state during those two decades,” the professor explains.
« Je pense que les gens font d’Haïti une: “I think people make an exception of Haiti. They don’t see how similar American policies are for Haiti, Iraq, Libya and other countries in terms of political destabilization and putting hand-picked candidates in power.”
M<sup>me</sup> Pierre en veut pour preuv: M<sup>s</sup>. Pierre points to the demonization of former president Jean-Bertrand Aristide, in power in 1991, from 1994 to 1996 and again from 2001 to 2004, and to the way the United States, France and other world powers drove him from power as proof.
« Il y a un essai intitulé <em>Comment t: “There’s an essay called Comment transformer un prêtre en cannibale, about how the media demonized him and made him the worst person on Earth,” she says.
L’argent de l’aide internationale finit: International aid money ends up being given to international organizations rather than to local NGOs and the government, Professor Pierre explains. These organizations have enormous power over Haiti’s political organization.
« Vous avez donc un processus où les ONG: “So you have a process where international NGOs hold more power than the state and determine what is covered, what kinds of health services are subsidized, for example,” says M<sup>s</sup>. Pierre.
La mainmise des États-Unis devient une n: The U.S. stranglehold became apparent once again a year after the infamous 2010 earthquake, which killed 200,000 people. Elections were held. Unhappy with the result of the first round, then-Secretary of State <l1>Hillary Clinton travelled to the island nation to insist</l1> that Michel Martelly be on the ballot for the second round. That intervention is said to have contributed to Mr. Martelly’s success and his election as president.
« En gros, Michel Martelly essaie essent: “Basically, Michel Martelly is essentially trying to sell off Haitian land and privatize everything,” explains M<sup>s</sup>. Pierre. These practices sparked numerous mass protests in 2018 and 2019. “Millions of people took to the streets against corruption. And it’s around that time that the political elites arm groups.”
Elle explique que les élites utilisent d: She explains that the elites use armed groups to fight one another and to fight people in working-class neighbourhoods. “The elites are used to using armed young men to go after their rivals in Haiti. If one family wanted to oppose another, using armed young men has always existed, but it multiplied after Martelly, who was well known for it. And then Jovenel Moïse made things worse.”
Devant la situation instable, la profess: Faced with the unstable situation, Professor Jemima Pierre points out that we also need to be careful about the words we use. She wants the media to stop using the word “gang” to describe the young men who, armed to the teeth, are storming Port-au-Prince.
« L’État utilise le terme \"gang\" pour: “The state uses the term ‘gang’ to comment on popular protests, and now you have people, including Western media, saying these gangs are everywhere,” she says.
« Mais ces gens ont été armés par des go: “But these people were armed by illegitimate governments, which the United States, the UN and other foreign powers have helped.”
Ottawa, hiver 2003. Une rencontre secrèt: Ottawa, winter 2003. A secret meeting, held on Canada’s initiative, takes place. The political fate of Haiti is debated… without Haiti. Journalist Michel Vastel of L’Actualité reveals what was said: leaders from Canada – Jean Chrétien at the time –, the United States, Germany, France and El Salvador conclude that President Aristide must go.
Vingt ans plus tard, un Sommet Canada-CA: Twenty years later, a Canada-CARICOM Summit takes place in Ottawa in October 2023, then more recently on March 1, 2024. It was after this meeting in Jamaica, led by Canada, that Ariel Henry resigned. Unpopular, he ultimately gave in to the pressure.
« Comment se fait-il que l’un des trois: “How is it that one of the three main countries responsible for destabilizing the country in 2004 (destabilization that led to the end of Jean-Bertrand Aristide’s government) is leading the negotiations in Jamaica to decide Haiti’s future?” asks Jemima Pierre.
« Le Canada joue un rôle important dans: “Canada plays an important role in political interference in Haiti. <l1>There are Canadian mining companies on the territory.</l1> In that sense, it’s not a question of ‘gangs,’ but a question of resources,” says Frantz André, skeptical about what the CARICOM meetings will yield. “I have little hope,” he says.
Pour l’heure, le Canada a évacué jeudi l: For now, Canada on Thursday evacuated most of its <l1>diplomatic staff</l1> and transferred them to neighbouring Dominican Republic. It is hard to predict what comes next, as a presidential council is to be appointed to oversee the transition.
Au Canada, on compte environ 165 000 res: In Canada, there are about 165,000 Haitian nationals. But to date, the Haitian diaspora has not organized a single demonstration. “We should see at least 5,000 people in the streets,” says Frantz André.
Il mentionne les appréhensions des gens,: He mentions people’s apprehensions: they fear being identified, which would endanger their family who stayed on the island. “So we’re seeing a kind of paralysis where no one takes part openly in certain initiatives, when we need to put pressure on Ottawa and Quebec City,” he believes.
Il espère qu'à Haïti, une force policièr: He hopes that a police force will be established in Haiti that the people can count on. For now, it is hard to see how that could happen without a government democratically elected by the people.
Par ailleurs, Frantz André note qu’une h: Frantz André also notes that an increase in asylum claims from Haitian nationals is to be expected.
« Ce qu’on voit, c’est une aggravation d: “What we’re seeing is the worsening of a situation that began 20 years ago. And it’s going to get worse. And it doesn’t help when everyone can see there are secret meetings in Jamaica with all these foreigners telling Haitians what their new government will look like,” says Jemima Pierre. “Right now, Haitians don’t want to see that anymore.”
M<sup>me</sup> Pierre souligne aussi que: M<sup>s</sup>. Pierre also stresses that the images playing on a loop, showing tires or other objects burning, are not necessarily a sign of chaos or of garbage overrunning the capital’s streets. “It’s often a strategy used by people in working-class neighbourhoods to protect the edge of their territory,” she clarifies.
Entre-temps, l’inquiétude persiste pour: In the meantime, worry persists for Frantz André, Monique and Jean Sadrac, who constantly fear for the health and safety of their loved ones.
« Quand mes proches m’appellent pour me: “When my loved ones call me to say they can’t take it anymore, that they’re unable to breathe, it’s as if inside me, something is tearing apart,” says Mr. Sadrac.
